description: We’re a small student-led team interested in using technology to solve real-world problems. I bring experience in Python, software development, AI/ML, and data analysis, and we’re excited to explore NASA’s open data and build a practical solution. We’re especially looking to collaborate with someone who enjoys Earth or space science, data visualization, UI/UX design, or communicating ideas clearly.
summary:
Environmental change is not uniform across a region. Regional averages can hide locations where temperature, precipitation or soil moisture are changing differently.

EarthTrend Lens is an interactive web application that helps users investigate these patterns by selecting two geographic regions and comparing historical NASA environmental data. It combines monthly time-series charts with maps showing period-average conditions and estimated spatial trends, allowing users to examine both how environmental variables change over time and where those changes occur.

The platform uses NASA POWER data for temperature and precipitation, alongside NASA GLDAS Noah 2.1 model estimates for root-zone soil moisture. Theil–Sen slope estimation is used to examine the direction and rate of historical trends.

Designed for environmental researchers, students and educators, EarthTrend Lens makes historical environmental data easier to explore and compare. It supports scientific investigation, not future prediction or causal attribution.
details:
1. Project Overview

EarthTrend Lens is an interactive geospatial platform developed to investigate historical environmental changes across different geographic regions. It connects temporal analysis with spatial visualisation, allowing users to compare two geographic study domains using NASA Earth-system datasets.

Instead of relying exclusively on broad regional averages, the platform allows users to explore time-series behaviour and spatial variations across individual geographic grid cells.

2. How It Works

EarthTrend Lens provides four connected workspaces:

  • 1. Investigate: Users select two geographic study domains, choose an environmental variable and define a historical period. The application retrieves the corresponding datasets and prepares the selected regions for comparison.
  • 2. Analysis: Users inspect monthly time series, anomaly views and estimated environmental trends. The analysis interface includes Theil–Sen slope estimation to examine the magnitude and direction of historical change.
  • 3. Spatial Explorer: Georeferenced raster layers display the spatial distribution of environmental variables and estimated trends. Users can compare the two domains, switch between Period Mean and Trend views, change basemaps, adjust layer opacity and inspect numerical colour legends.
  • 4. Data & Methods: The application documents dataset provenance, variable definitions, units, spatial resolutions, processing methods and scientific limitations.
3. NASA Data Sources

The platform uses two principal NASA data sources:

  • NASA POWER / MERRA-2
    • T2M: Near-surface air temperature (°C).
    • PRECTOTCORR: Corrected precipitation (mm/day).
    • Meteorological data derived from NASA's MERRA-2 modelling and assimilation system.
    • RootMoist_inst: Model-derived root-zone soil moisture (kg/m²).
    • Native spatial resolution: 0.25° × 0.25°.
    • DOI: 10.5067/SXAVCZFAQLNO.

The validated historical preset configurations cover January 2000 through December 2024, representing 300 monthly time steps. The datasets retain their respective source characteristics and spatial resolutions rather than being treated as equivalent direct measurements.

4. Scientific Processing and Methods

The application connects monthly environmental data with temporal and spatial analysis. Key methods include:

  • Temporal processing and monthly anomaly analysis.
  • Theil–Sen median pairwise slope estimation for examining trend magnitude and direction.
  • Generation of georeferenced raster outputs for spatial visualisation.
  • Comparative inspection of two geographic domains using shared variable and display settings.

Statistical Note: Statistical outputs, including p-value diagnostics where displayed by the application, should be interpreted according to the assumptions of their respective tests. They do not independently establish causation or guarantee future environmental conditions. Visual interpolation used for map presentation does not increase the native resolution of the source datasets.

5. Benefits and Intended Impact
  • Environmental research: Helps users investigate spatial variations alongside historical time-series behaviour.
  • Water-resource analysis: Provides historical precipitation and model-derived soil-moisture patterns as exploratory context.
  • Education: Makes NASA Earth-system data, geographic comparisons and statistical trend methods more accessible to students and educators.

The platform encourages users to examine not only how environmental variables change over time, but also where those changes occur geographically.

6. Technology and Architecture
  • Frontend: React 19, TypeScript, Vite and Tailwind CSS.
  • Mapping & Visualisation: Leaflet.js and Plotly.
  • Backend: Python and FastAPI.
  • Scientific processing: NumPy, SciPy, Numba, and geospatial raster-processing libraries.
  • Deployment: Live on Render.

The frontend communicates with the backend to retrieve and display processed environmental data and spatial raster outputs.

7. Creative Approach

The core concept is a dual-domain comparative investigation. Users can examine two geographic regions under a shared variable and historical period, switching between period-mean distributions and estimated trends.

Combining temporal charts, interactive spatial rasters and accessible dataset documentation provides a connected way to investigate environmental patterns without requiring users to build separate analysis scripts.

8. Scientific Considerations and Limitations
  • GLDAS Noah 2.1 soil-moisture values are land-surface model estimates, not direct in-situ measurements.
  • The NASA datasets have different native spatial resolutions.
  • The effective root-zone depth represented by GLDAS depends on the model's vegetation representation and is not a fixed 0–100 cm soil layer.
  • Spatial visualisation does not create additional source-data resolution.
  • Statistical inference must account for the assumptions of the selected tests, including possible seasonality and temporal autocorrelation.
  • Historical trends do not establish causal relationships or predict future environmental conditions.
  • EarthTrend Lens is an exploratory scientific investigation platform rather than an operational environmental forecasting or warning system.
  • Live application: https://earthtrend-lens.onrender.com/
  • Source code: https://github.com/Ravichandranayakar/earthtrend-lens
